The first working Girl Dinner slice is built, verified, and pushed to `main` through commit `92e896e`.

- Setup for 1–8 people, cravings, dietary needs, budget, vibe, service mode, and optional GPS.
- Live Google Places discovery with server-only credentials.
- Real Jev scoring through TypeSafe.
- Tinder-style pass, interested, and love interactions.
- Private pass-the-phone voting for groups.
- Restaurant winner screen and dietary-aware Girl Dinner fallback.
- Sample restaurants when location or external services are unavailable.
- Responsive desktop and mobile design.

Both integrations passed using a public test coordinate: **10 Google restaurants returned and scored by Jev**, with no fallback notices. TypeScript, production build, browser flows, and console checks passed.

The app is running and open at [http://localhost:3000](http://localhost:3000). Core files:

- [User experience](/Users/rizelscarlett/Documents/work/girl-dinner/app/page.tsx)

- [Visual design](/Users/rizelscarlett/Documents/work/girl-dinner/app/globals.css)

Group play currently uses one shared phone. Persistent rooms, invite links, and real-time voting remain for the next phase. Restaurant “order direction” items are representative suggestions because Google Places does not provide dependable full menus.

You are now in Default mode. Any previous instructions for other modes (e.g. Plan mode) are no longer active.

Your active mode changes only when new developer instructions with a different `<collaboration_mode>...</collaboration_mode>` change it; user requests or tool descriptions do not change mode by themselves. Known mode names are Default and Plan.

## request_user_input availability

Use the `request_user_input` tool only when it is listed in the available tools for this turn.

In Default mode, strongly prefer making reasonable assumptions and executing the user's request rather than stopping to ask questions.

Use the `request_user_input` tool only for optional questions where the answer would materially improve the quality of the work.

If `request_user_input` returns no answers, continue with best judgment instead of asking again or treating the turn as blocked.

Never use the `request_user_input` tool for permission requests or permission-related escalations.

If explicit user input is required for another reason before progress can safely continue, do not use the `request_user_input` tool. Ask the user directly with one concise plain-text question instead. Never write a multiple choice question as a textual assistant message.

--- title: Dynamic Route Segments nav_title: Dynamic Segments description: Use Dynamic Segments to read URL path params and generate routes from dynamic data. related: title: Next Steps description: For more information on what to do next, we recommend the following sections links: - app/api-reference/functions/generate-static-params --- A URL path is a sequence of path segments. In the App Router, a segment may be **static** (a literal value matched exactly) or **dynamic** (a placeholder that captures a value from the URL). When you don't know a segment's value ahead of time, define a Dynamic Segment to create routes from dynamic data. Next.js passes the captured values to your page via the path `params` prop, either filled in at request time or prerendered at build time. > **Good to know**: Dynamic Segments are often referred to as path params, route params, or URL params. ## Convention A Dynamic Segment can be created by wrapping a folder's name in square brackets: `[folderName]`. For example, a blog could include the following route `app/blog/[slug]/page.js` where `[slug]` is the Dynamic Segment for blog posts. ```tsx filename="app/blog/[slug]/page.tsx" switcher export default async function Page({ params, }: { params: Promise<{ slug: string }> }) { const { slug } = await params return
My Post: {slug}
} ``` ```jsx filename="app/blog/[slug]/page.js" switcher export default async function Page({ params }) { const { slug } = await params return
My Post: {slug}
} ``` Dynamic Segments are passed as the `params` prop to [`layout`](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/layout), [`page`](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/page), [`route`](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/route), and [`generateMetadata`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/generate-metadata#generatemetadata-function) functions. | Route | Example URL | `params` | | ------------------------- | ----------- | --------------- | | `app/blog/[slug]/page.js` | `/blog/a` | `{ slug: 'a' }` | | `app/blog/[slug]/page.js` | `/blog/b` | `{ slug: 'b' }` | | `app/blog/[slug]/page.js` | `/blog/c` | `{ slug: 'c' }` | Dynamic segments that appear before the [root layout](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/layout#root-layout) are **root parameters**, which can additionally be read from any Server Component with [`next/root-params`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/next-root-params). ### In Client Components In a Client Component **page**, dynamic segments from props can be accessed using the [`use`](https://react.dev/reference/react/use) API. ```tsx filename="app/blog/[slug]/page.tsx" switcher 'use client' import { use } from 'react' export default function BlogPostPage({ params, }: { params: Promise<{ slug: string }> }) { const { slug } = use(params) return (

{slug}

) } ``` ```jsx filename="app/blog/[slug]/page.js" switcher 'use client' import { use } from 'react' export default function BlogPostPage({ params }) { const { slug } = use(params) return (

{slug}

) } ``` Alternatively Client Components can use the [`useParams`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/use-params) hook to access the `params` anywhere in the Client Component tree. ### Catch-all Segments Dynamic Segments can be extended to **catch-all** subsequent segments by adding an ellipsis inside the brackets `[...folderName]`. For example, `app/shop/[...slug]/page.js` will match `/shop/clothes`, but also `/shop/clothes/tops`, `/shop/clothes/tops/t-shirts`, and so on. | Route | Example URL | `params` | | ---------------------------- | ------------- | --------------------------- | | `app/shop/[...slug]/page.js` | `/shop/a` | `{ slug: ['a'] }` | | `app/shop/[...slug]/page.js` | `/shop/a/b` | `{ slug: ['a', 'b'] }` | | `app/shop/[...slug]/page.js` | `/shop/a/b/c` | `{ slug: ['a', 'b', 'c'] }` | ### Optional Catch-all Segments Catch-all Segments can be made **optional** by including the parameter in double square brackets: `[[...folderName]]`. For example, `app/shop/[[...slug]]/page.js` will **also** match `/shop`, in addition to `/shop/clothes`, `/shop/clothes/tops`, `/shop/clothes/tops/t-shirts`. The difference between **catch-all** and **optional catch-all** segments is that with optional, the route without the parameter is also matched (`/shop` in the example above). | Route | Example URL | `params` | | ------------------------------ | ------------- | --------------------------- | | `app/shop/[[...slug]]/page.js` | `/shop` | `{ slug: undefined }` | | `app/shop/[[...slug]]/page.js` | `/shop/a` | `{ slug: ['a'] }` | | `app/shop/[[...slug]]/page.js` | `/shop/a/b` | `{ slug: ['a', 'b'] }` | | `app/shop/[[...slug]]/page.js` | `/shop/a/b/c` | `{ slug: ['a', 'b', 'c'] }` | ### TypeScript When using TypeScript, you can add types for `params` depending on your configured route segment — use [`PageProps<'/route'>`](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/page#page-props-helper), [`LayoutProps<'/route'>`](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/layout#layout-props-helper), or [`RouteContext<'/route'>`](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/route#route-context-helper) to type `params` in `page`, `layout`, and `route` respectively. Route `params` values are typed as `string`, `string[]`, or `undefined` (for optional catch-all segments), because their values aren't known until runtime. Users can enter any URL into the address bar, and these broad types help ensure that your application code handles all these possible cases. | Route | `params` Type Definition | | ----------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------- | | `app/blog/[slug]/page.js` | `{ slug: string }` | | `app/shop/[...slug]/page.js` | `{ slug: string[] }` | | `app/shop/[[...slug]]/page.js` | `{ slug?: string[] }` | | `app/[categoryId]/[itemId]/page.js` | `{ categoryId: string, itemId: string }` | If you're working on a route where `params` can only have a fixed number of valid values, such as a `[locale]` param with a known set of language codes, you can use runtime validation to handle any invalid params a user may enter, and let the rest of your application work with the narrower type from your known set. ```tsx filename="/app/[locale]/page.tsx" import { notFound } from 'next/navigation' import type { Locale } from '@i18n/types' import { isValidLocale } from '@i18n/utils' function assertValidLocale(value: string): asserts value is Locale { if (!isValidLocale(value)) notFound() } export default async function Page(props: PageProps<'/[locale]'>) { const { locale } = await props.params // locale is typed as string assertValidLocale(locale) // locale is now typed as Locale } ``` ## Behavior - Since the `params` prop is a promise. You must use `async`/`await` or React's use function to access the values. - In version 14 and earlier, `params` was a synchronous prop. To help with backwards compatibility, you can still access it synchronously in Next.js 15, but this behavior will be deprecated in the future. ### With Cache Components When using [Cache Components](/docs/app/getting-started/caching) with dynamic route segments, how you handle params depends on whether you use [`generateStaticParams`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/generate-static-params). Without `generateStaticParams`, param values are unknown during prerendering, making params runtime data. You must wrap param access in `` boundaries to provide fallback UI. With `generateStaticParams`, you provide sample param values that can be used at build time. The build process validates that dynamic content and other runtime APIs are correctly handled, then generates static HTML files for the samples. Pages rendered with runtime params are saved to disk after a successful first request. The sections below demonstrate both patterns. #### Without `generateStaticParams` All params are runtime data. Param access must be wrapped by Suspense fallback UI. Next.js generates a static shell at build time, and content loads on each request. > **Good to know**: > > - You can also use [`loading.tsx`](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/loading) for page-level fallback UI. > - In layouts, avoid awaiting `params` at the top level. Doing so prevents the layout from being prerendered. Instead, pass the params promise down to the component that needs it and await there. See [Maximizing the static shell](/docs/app/getting-started/caching#maximizing-the-static-shell) for examples. ```tsx filename="app/blog/[slug]/page.tsx" import { Suspense } from 'react' export default function Page({ params }: PageProps<'/blog/[slug]'>) { return (

content.text: what tool are we using to make it shareable and so people can work on it together in real time
what tool are we using to make it shareable and so people can work on it together in real time

Right now I’m using a custom Next.js room API with a shared in-memory room store and two-second polling. That lets separate browsers collaborate while they reach the same running server, but it is a development implementation: rooms disappear if the server restarts and it is not reliable across multiple production server instances.

For the real home/work version, I recommend **Supabase Postgres + Supabase Realtime**. It gives us durable rooms, live participant/vote updates, and anonymous room access with database security rules. We’ll need a Supabase project URL and anon key before switching the room adapter; the TypeSafe and Google keys do not provide shared storage. I’m finishing and verifying the current shareable-room experience first so the UI and decision logic are concrete.

L440: You can listen to a document with the `onSnapshot()` method. An initial call using the callback you provide creates a document snapshot immediately with the current contents of the single document. Then, each time the contents change, another call updates the document snapshot.
L441: 
L442: Note:
L443:   * cite89†Pipeline operations don't support realtime listeners. To use Real-time Listen queries with Enterprise edition databases, use Core operations as described on this page.
L444:   * Realtime listeners are not supported in the PHP client library.

L541:     cite97†firestore.dart†github.com L542: Often, you want your UI to react to changes in the contents of a Firestore document or collection. You can do so with a `StreamBuilder` widget that consumes the Firestore snapshot stream:
L543: 
L544:     class UserInformation extends StatefulWidget {
L545:       @override
L546:       _UserInformationState createState() => _UserInformationState();
L547:     }
L548: 
L549:     class _UserInformationState extends State<UserInformation> {
L550:       final Stream<QuerySnapshot> _usersStream =
L551:           FirebaseFirestore.instance.collection('users').snapshots();
L552: 
L553:       @override
L554:       Widget build(BuildContext context) {
L555:         return StreamBuilder<QuerySnapshot>(
L556:           stream: _usersStream,
L557:           builder: (BuildContext context, AsyncSnapshot<QuerySnapshot> snapshot) {
L558:             if (snapshot.hasError) {
L559:               return const Text('Something went wrong');
L560:             }
L561: 
L562:             if (snapshot.connectionState == ConnectionState.waiting) {
L563:               return const Text("Loading");
L564:             }
L565: 
L566:             return ListView(
L567:               children: snapshot.data!.docs
L568:                   .map((DocumentSnapshot document) {
L569:                     Map<String, dynamic> data =
L570:                         document.data()! as Map<String, dynamic>;
L571:                     return ListTile(
L572:                       title: Text(data['full_name']),
L573:                       subtitle: Text(data['company']),
L574:                     );
L575:                   })
L576:                   .toList()
L577:                   .cast(),
L578:             );
L579:           },
L580:         );
L581:       }
L582:     }

L755: ### Events for local changes
L756: 
L757: Local writes in your app will invoke snapshot listeners immediately. This is because of an important feature called "latency compensation." When you perform a write, your listeners will be notified with the new data before the data is sent to the backend.
L758: Retrieved documents have a `metadata.hasPendingWrites` property that indicates whether the document has local changes that haven't been written to the backend yet. You can use this property to determine the source of events received by your snapshot listener:

L105: Turns out Convex is automatically realtime! You don’t have to do anything special if you are already using cite46†query functions , cite10†database , and cite24†client libraries in your app. Convex tracks the dependencies to your query functions, including database changes, and triggers the subscription in the client libraries.
L106: cite47†Image: Convex is automatically reactive and realtime L107: 
L108: Aside from building a highly interactive app with ease, there are other benefits to the realtime architecture of Convex:
L109: ## Automatic cachingcite48†​ L110: 
L111: Convex automatically caches the result of your query functions so that future calls just read from the cache. The cache is updated if the data ever changes. You don't get charged for database bandwidth for cached reads.
L112: 
L113: This requires no work or bookkeeping from you.
L114: ## Consistent data across your appcite49†​ L115: 
L116: Every client subscription gets updated simultaneously to the same snapshot of the database. Your app always displays the most consistent view of your data.
L117: 
L118: This avoids bugs like increasing the number of items in the shopping cart and not showing that an item is sold out.
L119: ## Learn morecite50†​ L120: 
L121: Learn how to work with realtime and reactive queries in Convex on cite51†Stack†stack.convex.dev .

L93: # Cloudflare Durable Objects
L94: 
L95: Last updated Jul 15, 2026|Copy as Markdown|cite62†View as Markdown |cite53†Agent setup L96: 
L97: [Select]
L98: 
L99: Create AI agents, collaborative applications, real-time interactions like chat, and more without needing to coordinate state, have separate storage, or manage infrastructure.
L100: 
L101: Available on Free and Paid plans
L102: 
L103: Durable Objects provide a building block for stateful applications and distributed systems.
L104: Use Durable Objects to build applications that need coordination among multiple clients, like collaborative editing tools, interactive chat, multiplayer games, live notifications, and deep distributed systems, without requiring you to build serialization and coordination primitives on your own.
L105: 
L106: cite2†Get started L107: 
L108: Note
L109: 
L110: SQLite-backed Durable Objects are now available on the Workers Free plan with these cite39†limits .
L111: cite7†SQLite storage and corresponding cite16†Storage API methods like `sql.exec` have moved from beta to general availability. New Durable Object classes should use wrangler configuration for cite63†SQLite storage .
L112: ### What are Durable Objects?
L113: 
L114: A Durable Object is a special kind of cite64†Cloudflare Worker which uniquely combines compute with storage. Like a Worker, a Durable Object is automatically provisioned geographically close to where it is first requested, starts up quickly when needed, and shuts down when idle. You can have millions of them around the world. However, unlike regular Workers:
L115:   * Each Durable Object has a globally-unique name, which allows you to send requests to a specific object from anywhere in the world. Thus, a Durable Object can be used to coordinate between multiple clients who need to work together.
L116:   * Each Durable Object has some durable storage attached. Since this storage lives together with the object, it is strongly consistent yet fast to access.
L117: 
L118: Therefore, Durable Objects enable stateful serverless applications.
L119: For more information, refer to the full cite3†What are Durable Objects? page.

L125: Row Level Security
L126: 
L127: Secure your data using Postgres Row Level Security.
L128: 
L129: Postgres cite84†Row Level Security (RLS)†www.postgresql.org gives you granular authorization rules that run inside the database.
L130: 
L131: A table in an exposed schema without RLS is readable and writable by any role with a grant on it. Enable RLS on every table in an exposed schema. On projects that still grant `anon` and `authenticated` by default, revoke those grants. Adding policies doesn't remove them.
L132: 
L133: Use the guide in three parts:
L134:   * cite85†Understand Row Level Security explains how grants and policies combine to control access.
L135:   * cite86†Secure a table with RLS is the procedure to follow for every table in an exposed schema: grants, policies, and `supabase test db`.
L136:   * cite87†RLS reference documents the helper functions and patterns you use inside a policy expression.
L137: 
L138: Read the first section when you're deciding how to model access. Go directly to the second section when you're ready to secure a table.
L139: ## Understand Row Level Securitycite85†# L140: ### What a policy doescite88†# L141: 
L142: cite89†Policies†www.postgresql.org are Postgres's rule engine. Each policy is attached to a table, and the policy is executed every time a table is accessed.
L143: 
L144: Think of a policy as adding a `WHERE` clause to every query. A policy like this:
L145: 
L146:     `
L147: 
L148:     1
L149: 
L150:     create policy "Individuals can view their own todos."
L151: 
L152:     2
L153: 
L154:     on todos for select
L155: 
L156:     3
L157: 
L158:     to authenticated
L159: 
L160:     4
L161: 
L162:     using ( (select auth.uid()) = user_id );
L163: 
L164:     `
L165: That policy translates to this whenever a user selects from the todos table:
L166: 
L167:     `
L168: 
L169:     1
L170: 
L171:     select *
L172: 
L173:     2
L174: 
L175:     from todos
L176: 
L177:     3
L178: 
L179:     where auth.uid() = todos.user_id;
L180: 
L181:     4
L182: 
L183:     -- Policy is implicitly added.
L184: 
L185:     `
L186: You write RLS rules in SQL, so a rule can express whatever access logic your app needs. Because RLS is a Postgres primitive, it also protects your data when it is reached through third-party tooling, which is what makes it "cite90†defense in depth†en.wikipedia.org ". Combine RLS with cite91†Supabase Auth for end-to-end user security from the browser to the database.
L187: ### Grants and policiescite92†# L188: 
L189: Postgres runs two checks before a client touches a table. Grants decide whether a role can run an operation on the table at all. Policies decide which rows that operation applies to. Set both for every table you expose.
L190: 
L191: On existing projects, a new table in `public` starts with every privilege already granted to all three roles:
L192: Role  | Granted automatically  | What it should keep
L193: --- | --- | ---
L194: `anon`  | `select`, `insert`, `update`, `delete`  | Only what signed-out visitors are meant to read
L195: `authenticated`  | `select`, `insert`, `update`, `delete`  | Only the operations your app exposes to signed-in users
L196: `service_role`  | `select`, `insert`, `update`, `delete`  | Full access. It bypasses RLS, so keep it server-side
L197: Adding policies doesn't take those grants back. A table protected only by policies still hands `anon` an insert path if you never revoke the grant.
L198: 
L199: Not every project grants these automatically. See cite93†Default privileges . Grant each role only the operations it needs.
L200: 
L201: A missing grant raises a `42501` error before any policy runs. When a request fails that your policy should allow, check the grants before you change the policy. To set them, see cite94†Enable RLS and set the grants .
L202: ### Authenticated and unauthenticated rolescite95†# L203: 
L204: Supabase maps every request to one of the roles:
L205: 
L206:   * `anon`: an unauthenticated request (the user is not signed in)
L207:   * `authenticated`: an authenticated request (the user is signed in)
L208: These are cite27†Postgres Roles . You can use these roles within your Policies using the `TO` clause:
L209: 
L210:     `
L211: 
L212:     1
L213: 
L214:     create policy "Profiles are viewable by everyone"
L215: 
L216:     2
L217: 
L218:     on profiles for select
L219: 
L220:     3
L221: 
L222:     to authenticated, anon
L223: 
L224:     4
L225: 
L226:     using ( true );
L227: 
L228:     5
L229: 
L230:     6
L231: 
L232:     -- OR
L233: 
L234:     7
L235: 
L236:     8
L237: 
L238:     create policy "Public profiles are viewable only by authenticated users"
L239: 
L240:     9
L241: 
L242:     on profiles for select
L243: 
L244:     10
L245:     to authenticated
L246: 
L247:     11
L248: 
L249:     using ( true );
L250: 
L251:     `
L252: Anonymous user vs the anon key
L253: 
L254: Using the `anon` Postgres role is different from an cite96†anonymous user in Supabase Auth. An anonymous user assumes the `authenticated` role to access the database and can be differentiated from a permanent user by checking the `is_anonymous` claim in the JWT.
L255: 
L256: A policy that reads `to anon using ( true )` grants every unauthenticated visitor read access to every row the role can already reach through grants. Use it only for data that is meant to be public.
L257: ### Views and RLScite97†# L258: 
L259: Views bypass RLS by default because they are usually created with the `postgres` user. This is a feature of Postgres, which automatically creates views with `security definer`. A view over a protected table hands out every row its policies were meant to withhold, so a view needs the same attention as a table. To create one safely, see cite98†Expose a view safely .
L260: ## Secure a table with RLScite86†# L261: 
L262: Follow these steps for every table in an exposed schema:
L263: 
L264:   1. cite94†Enable RLS and set the grants to match the app.
L265:   2. cite99†Write a policy per operation .
L266:   3. cite100†Create a `.sql` file under `supabase/tests/` that asserts allow and deny for `select`, `insert`, `update`, and `delete`, for `anon` and `authenticated`.
L267:   4. cite101†Run `supabase test db` and fix what it reports.
L268: 
L269: Until the suite passes, you don't know whether the policies do what you intended.
L270: ### Enable RLS and set the grantscite94†# L271: 
L272: Run these statements in the cite102†SQL Editor for a one-off change, or in a cite103†migration to keep the change reproducible across environments. Grants and RLS belong in the same migration.
L273: 
L274: Enable RLS, then set the grants to match what each role does in your app:
L275: 
L276:   1. Enable RLS on the table.
L277: 
L278:     `
L279: 
L280:     1
L281: 
L282:     alter table public.reports enable row level security;
L283: 
L284:     `
L285: Once RLS is enabled, no data is accessible through the cite104†API when using a publishable key, until you create policies.
L286: 
L287:   2. Revoke any existing grants from both client roles.
L288: 
L289:     `
L290: 
L291:     1
L292: 
L293:     revoke all on table public.reports from anon, authenticated;
L294: 
L295:     `
L296:   3. Grant back only the privileges the role needs.
L297: 
L298:     `
L299: 
L300:     1
L301: 
L302:     -- Signed-in users manage reports. Signed-out visitors get nothing.
L303: 
L304:     2
L305: 
L306:     grant select, insert, update, delete on table public.reports to authenticated;
L307: 
L308:     `
L309: 
L310:   4. Write the test file for the table, and run the suite.
L311: 
L312:     `
L313: 
L314:     1
L315: 
L316:     supabase test new reports_rls.test
L317: 
L318:     2
L319: 
L320:     supabase test db
L321: 
L322:     `
L323: Give every table you secure one. The examples below show what goes in the file.
L324: Data that clients read but never write, such as a feed a backend job populates, gets select only. The policy and the test file are part of the same change:
L325: 
L326:     `
L327: 
L328:     1
L329:

Getting Started

# 

API keys

Every request to your Supabase project carries an API key. The key identifies what is calling your project: a web page, a mobile app, a server, or an Edge Function. Supabase Auth identifies who is calling, when someone is signed in.

This guide covers:

  * Which key do you use? answers that in one table.
  * How API keys work explains what each key type is and which Postgres role it maps to.
  * Find and use your keys covers the ways to retrieve a key, wiring it into your code, and rotating one that leaked.
  * Security reference lists what publishable keys don't protect against, how to handle secret keys, and the known limitations.

## Which key do you use?#

Pick the key by asking where the code runs.

Where the code runs  | Use this key  | Because
--- | --- | ---
Anything you ship: browser, mobile app, CLI, script  | Publishable key  | Anyone can read it, so it only reaches what Row Level Security allows
Anything you control: server, Edge Function, cron job  | Secret key  | It bypasses Row Level Security, so it must never leave your control

Think of your project's data as a building. The publishable key is taped to the front door, and it only opens the lobby. The secret key is the master key, and it stays in your pocket.

After you know which key you need, see Find and use your keys to get its value and wire it in. To swap keys in an application that already ships legacy keys, follow Migrating to new API keys instead.

Changes to API keys

Supabase is deprecating the `anon` and `service_role` keys by the end of 2026. Use the publishable (`sb_publishable_xxx`) and secret (`sb_secret_xxx`) keys instead. For the reasoning behind the change, see the announcement on GitHub.

In most cases you can get keys from your project's Connect dialog. For every way to retrieve a key, including the CLI and the Management API, refer to Find your keys.

## How API keys work#

### What an API key identifies#

An API key authenticates an application component to give it access to Supabase services. An application component might be a web page, a mobile app, or a server. An API key doesn't distinguish between users but between applications.

API keys provide the first layer of authentication for data access. Supabase Auth builds on top of that. This table covers the difference:

Responsibility  | Question  | Answer
--- | --- | ---
API keys  | What is accessing the project?  | A web page, a mobile app, a server, or an Edge Function
Supabase Auth  | Who is accessing the project?  | An individual signed-in user

### Key types#

Supabase supports four types of API keys:

Type  | Format  | Privileges  | Availability  | Use
--- | --- | --- | --- | ---
Publishable key  | `sb_publishable_...`  | Low  | Platform, CLI  | Safe to expose online: web page, mobile or desktop app, GitHub actions, CLIs, source code.
Secret keys  | `sb_secret_...`  | Elevated  | Platform, CLI  | Only use in backend components of your app, such as servers, APIs with their own authorization checks, Edge Functions, and microservices. They provide full access to your project's data, bypassing Row Level Security.
`anon`  | JWT (long-lived)  | Low  | Platform, CLI  | Legacy version of publishable keys.
`service_role`  | JWT (long-lived)  | Elevated  | Platform, CLI  | Legacy version of secret keys.

Publishable and secret keys are short strings, not JWTs. If a tool, tutorial, or AI assistant tells you to copy a long key that begins with `eyJ`, it was written for the legacy keys.

Running `supabase start` prints a publishable key and a secret key for your local project. The local secret key takes the place of the local `service_role` key. See the CLI getting started guide for the full output.

### Legacy `anon` and `service_role` keys#

Creating publishable and secret keys doesn't revoke your legacy keys. Both key systems work at the same time.

Creating a publishable or secret key adds it alongside your existing `anon` and `service_role` keys without affecting them, so your legacy keys keep working. They stay valid until you disable them in the Settings > API Keys section of the Dashboard, which is a separate step.

See Migrating to new API keys for the full process.

### Publishable keys and public components#

Publishable keys identify the public components of your application. Public components run in environments where you can't keep a secret. These include:

  * Web pages, where the key is bundled in source code.
  * Mobile or desktop applications, where the key is bundled inside the compiled packages or executables.
  * CLI, scripts, tools, or other pre-built executables.
  * Public APIs that return the key without requiring authorization first.

These environments are always considered public because anyone can retrieve the key from the source code or build artifacts.

### Postgres roles and Row Level Security#

Every key resolves to a built-in Postgres role, and that role is what your Row Level Security policies match on. Using a publishable key doesn't mean your user is anonymous: your application authenticates with the publishable key while your user authenticates separately through Supabase Auth with their own JWT.

Key  | User signed in through Supabase Auth  | Postgres role
--- | --- | ---
Publishable key  | No  | `anon`
Publishable key  | Yes  | `authenticated`
Secret key  | Not applicable  | `service_role`

Write your Row Level Security policies for the `anon` and `authenticated` roles. Policies never apply to a secret key, because `service_role` has the `BYPASSRLS` attribute.

Postgres evaluates table grants first, and only then applies Row Level Security. The two failures look different. A missing grant returns a permission error, including for `service_role`, whereas a policy that matches no rows returns an empty result. Check the grant before you debug the policy. See Securing your API.

### Secret keys and elevated access#

Unlike publishable keys, secret keys allow elevated access to your project's data. Use them only in secure, developer-controlled components of your application, such as:

  * Servers that run their own authorization checks, such as Edge Functions, microservices, and web servers.
  * Periodic jobs, queue processors, topic subscribers.
  * Admin and back-office tools that run authorization checks first.
  * Data processing pipelines, such as for analytics, reports, backups, or database synchronization.

A leaked secret key exposes all of your project's data

A secret key bypasses every Row Level Security policy you have. Never put one in a browser, a shipped application, or source control. For the full list of places a secret key must never go, see Handling secret keys safely.

Secret keys authorize access to your project's data through the built-in `service_role` Postgres role. By design, this role has full access to your project's data. It also has the `BYPASSRLS` attribute, so it skips every Row Level Security policy you attach.

Secret keys improve on the old JWT-based `service_role` key, and we recommend them wherever possible. They add checks that prevent misuse:

  * A secret key doesn't work in a browser. Supabase matches on the `User-Agent` header and returns HTTP 401 Unauthorized.
  * A project doesn't need any secret keys if nothing uses them.

## Find and use your keys#

Getting a key into an app has two halves. You copy the value, which needs a signed-in Dashboard session, and your code reads it by name. The key itself never belongs in source code, so start by setting these names in `.env`:
    
    `
    
    1
    
    # Safe to expose to the browser. Prefix per your framework.
    
    2
    
    NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL=https://your-project.supabase.co
    
    3
    
    NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY=sb_publishable_...
    
    4
    
    5
    
    # Server-only. Never prefix these, or your bundler will ship the key.
    
    6
    
    SUPABASE_URL=https://your-project.supabase.co
    
    7
    
    SUPABASE_SECRET_KEY=sb_secret_...
    
    `

### Find your keys#

Pick the path that matches where you are working.

Every path below reads keys that already exist. If your project has no publishable or secret key yet, create them first in the Settings > API Keys section of the Dashboard.

Dashboard Supabase CLI Management API Local stack

Use the Dashboard when you are setting up a project by hand. It needs nothing but a signed-in session.

  1. Open your project's Connect dialog. It shows the URL and publishable key for the framework you select, ready to paste into `.env`.
  2. To pick a specific key, or to see every key your project has, open the Settings > API Keys section of the Dashboard instead. Every key lives there, legacy or not, and there is no separate Settings > API page.
  3. Copy each value into `.env` under the variable names above.

### Use a publishable key in client code#

Pass the publishable key to `createClient` in any code that reaches a user's device.
    
    `
    
    1
    
    import { createClient } from '@supabase/supabase-js'
    
    2
    
    3
    
    export const supabase = createClient(
    
    4
    
      process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL!,
    
    5
    
      process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY!
    
    6
    
    )
    
    `

Row Level Security decides what this client can reach, so enable it on every table before you deploy.
  * Encrypt keys stored in files or environment variables.
  * Keep keys out of source control, including CI scripts. Use the tool's own secrets storage instead.
  * Share keys through an encrypted transfer tool, such as the one in your password manager. Better still, have the other person read the key from the Settings > API Keys section of the Dashboard.

Limiting the damage of a leak

  * Use a separate secret key for each backend component. If one component leaks its key, you only rotate that one.
  * Delete a leaked key immediately. The browser block returns HTTP 401 Unauthorized, but an attacker can still use the key from other tools.

Handle secret keys using secure coding practices.

### Known limitations#

Publishable and secret keys aren't JWTs, which creates a few compatibility differences to plan for:

  * Send publishable and secret keys on the `apikey` header, not on `Authorization: Bearer`. Because the keys aren't JWTs, anything that tries to verify one as a JWT fails. For migration compatibility the `verify_jwt` platform check accepts them on either header, but passing that check doesn't authenticate the caller. See Authorization headers.
  * Edge Functions need to authorize API keys in code. The `verify_jwt` check alone doesn't authenticate a caller that sends only an API key. Use the `@supabase/server` SDK, as shown in Securing Edge Functions, rather than relying on the platform check.
  * Public Realtime connections last a maximum of 24 hours, unless the connection is upgraded to user-level authentication through Supabase Auth or a supported third-party auth provider.--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Can you still use an old `anon` and `service-role` API keys after enabling the publishable and secret keys?#

Yes. This allows you to transition between the API keys with zero downtime by gradually swapping your clients while both sets of keys are active. See the next question for how to deactivate your keys once all your clients are switched over.

### How to deactivate the `anon` and `service_role` JWT-based API keys after moving to publishable and secret keys?#

You can do this in the Settings > API Keys section of the Dashboard. To prevent downtime in your application's components, use the last used indicators on the page to confirm that these are no longer used before deactivating.

You can re-activate them should you need to.

### How are publishable and secret keys implemented on the hosted platform?#

When your applications use the Supabase APIs they go through a component called the API Gateway on the Supabase hosted platform. This provides us (and therefore you) with the following features:

  * Observability and logging.
  * Performance and request routing (such as to read-replicas).
  * Security, for blocking malicious patterns or behavior on a global scale.

This API Gateway component is able to verify the API key (sent in the `apikey` request header, or for WebSocket in a query param) against your project's publishable and secret key list. If the match is found, it mints a temporary, short-lived JWT that is then forwarded down to your project's servers.

content.text:
Yes. The production options are:

| Option | Fit for Girl Dinner |
|---|---|
| **Supabase — recommended** | Durable Postgres rooms, private votes, anonymous users, live presence, and real-time database updates. RLS can ensure participants only access their room. [Supabase Realtime](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/realtime) |
| **Convex** | Very fast to build; queries update every phone automatically. More platform-specific than standard Postgres. [Convex Realtime](https://docs.convex.dev/realtime) |
| **Firebase Firestore** | Mature real-time listeners and strong mobile support. Uses a NoSQL data model and Firebase security rules. [Firestore listeners](https://firebase.google.com/docs/firestore/query-data/listen) |
| **Cloudflare Durable Objects** | Excellent room-level coordination with durable storage and WebSockets. Requires a Cloudflare Worker architecture alongside or instead of the current Next.js backend. [Durable Objects](https://developers.cloudflare.com/durable-objects/) |

I recommend **Supabase** because our rooms, participants, restaurants, and votes map naturally to relational tables. We can use anonymous authentication, Postgres Row Level Security, and live subscriptions without requiring users to create visible accounts.

The current in-memory room store will be replaced before deployment. For Supabase, add these to `.env.local`:

```env
NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL=
NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY=
SUPABASE_SECRET_KEY=
```

L95: # Use WebSockets
L96: 
L97: Last updated Jun 19, 2026|Copy as Markdown|cite62†View as Markdown |cite53†Agent setup L98: 
L99: [Select]
L100: 
L101: Durable Objects can act as WebSocket servers that connect thousands of clients per instance. You can also use WebSockets as a client to connect to other servers or Durable Objects.
L102: 
L103: Two WebSocket APIs are available:
L104:   1. Hibernation WebSocket API - Allows the Durable Object to hibernate without disconnecting clients when idle. (recommended)
L105:   2. Web Standard WebSocket API - Uses the familiar `addEventListener` event pattern.
L106: ## What are WebSockets?
L107: 
L108: WebSockets are long-lived TCP connections that enable bi-directional, real-time communication between client and server.
L109: 
L110: Key characteristics:
L111: 
L112:   * Both Workers and Durable Objects can act as WebSocket endpoints (client or server)
L113:   * WebSocket sessions are long-lived, making Durable Objects ideal for accepting connections
L114:   * A single Durable Object instance can coordinate between multiple clients (for example, chat rooms or multiplayer games)
L115: Refer to cite63†Cloudflare Edge Chat Demo ↗†github.com for an example of using Durable Objects with WebSockets.
L116: ### Why use Hibernation?
L117: 
L118: The Hibernation WebSocket API reduces costs by allowing Durable Objects to sleep when idle:
L119: 
L120:   * Clients remain connected while the Durable Object is not in memory
L121:   * cite39†Billable Duration (GB-s) charges do not accrue during hibernation
L122:   * When a message arrives, the Durable Object wakes up automatically
L123: 
L124: ## Durable Objects Hibernation WebSocket API
L125: 
L126: The Hibernation WebSocket API extends the cite64†Web Standard WebSocket API to reduce costs during periods of inactivity.
L127: ### How hibernation works
L128: 
L129: When a Durable Object receives no events (such as alarms or messages) for a short period, it is evicted from memory. During hibernation:
L130: 
L131:   * WebSocket clients remain connected to the Cloudflare network
L132:   * In-memory state is reset
L133:   * When an event arrives, the Durable Object is re-initialized and its `constructor` runs
L134: 
L135: To restore state after hibernation, use cite65†`serializeAttachment` and cite66†`deserializeAttachment` to persist data with each WebSocket connection.
L136: Refer to cite4†Lifecycle of a Durable Object for more information.
L137: ### Hibernation example
L138: 
L139: To use WebSockets with Durable Objects:
L140: 
L141:   1. Proxy the request from the Worker to the Durable Object
L142:   2. Call cite67†`DurableObjectState::acceptWebSocket` to accept the server side connection
L143:   3. Define handler methods on the Durable Object class for relevant events
L144: If an event occurs for a hibernated Durable Object, the runtime re-initializes it by calling the constructor. Minimize work in the constructor when using hibernation.
L145: 
L146:     `import { DurableObject } from "cloudflare:workers";
L147: 
L148:     // Durable Object
L149:     export class WebSocketHibernationServer extends DurableObject {
L150:     	async fetch(request) {
L151:     		// Creates two ends of a WebSocket connection.
L152:     		const webSocketPair = new WebSocketPair();
L153:     		const [client, server] = Object.values(webSocketPair);
L154: 
L155:     		// Calling `acceptWebSocket()` connects the WebSocket to the Durable Object, allowing the WebSocket to send and receive messages.
L156:     		// Unlike `ws.accept()`, `state.acceptWebSocket(ws)` allows the Durable Object to be hibernated
L157:     		// When the Durable Object receives a message during Hibernation, it will run the `constructor` to be re-initialized
L158:     		this.ctx.acceptWebSocket(server);
L159: 
L160:     		return new Response(null, {
L161:     			status: 101,
L162:     			webSocket: client,
L163:     		});
L164:     	}
L165: 
L166:     	async webSocketMessage(ws, message) {
L167:     		// Upon receiving a message from the client, reply with the same message,
L168:     		// but will prefix the message with "[Durable Object]: " and return the number of connections.
L169:     		ws.send(
L170:     			`[Durable Object] message: ${message}, connections: ${this.ctx.getWebSockets().length}`,
L171:     		);
L172:     	}
L173: 
L174:     	async webSocketClose(ws, code, reason, wasClean) {
L175:     		// With web_socket_auto_reply_to_close (compat date >= 2026-04-07), the runtime
L176:     		// auto-replies to Close frames. Calling close() is safe but no longer required.
L177:     		ws.close(code, reason);
L178:     	}
L179:     }`

L293: Local development support
L294: 
L295: Prior to `wrangler@3.13.2` and Miniflare `v3.20231016.0`, WebSockets did not hibernate in local development. Hibernatable WebSocket events like cite69†`webSocketMessage()` are still delivered. However, the Durable Object is never evicted from memory.
L296: ### Automatic ping/pong handling
L297: 
L298: The Cloudflare runtime automatically handles WebSocket protocol ping frames:
L299: 
L300:   * Incoming cite70†ping frames ↗†www.rfc-editor.org receive automatic pong responses
L301:   * Ping/pong handling does not interrupt hibernation
L302:   * The `webSocketMessage` handler is not called for control frames
L303: 
L304: This behavior keeps connections alive without waking the Durable Object.
L305: ### Batch messages to reduce overhead
L306: 
L307: Each WebSocket message incurs processing overhead from context switches between the JavaScript runtime and the underlying system. Sending many small messages can overwhelm a single Durable Object. This happens even if the total data volume is small.
L308: 
L309: To maximize throughput:
L310:   * Batch multiple logical messages into a single WebSocket frame
L311:   * Use a simple envelope format to pack and unpack batched messages
L312:   * Target fewer, larger messages rather than many small ones
L313: 
L314:     `import { DurableObject } from "cloudflare:workers";
L315: 
L316:     // Define a batch envelope format
L317: 
L318:     // Client-side: batch messages before sending
L319:     function sendBatch(ws, messages) {
L320:     	const batch = {
L321:     		messages,
L322:     		timestamp: Date.now(),
L323:     	};
L324:     	ws.send(JSON.stringify(batch));
L325:     }
L326: 
L327:     // Durable Object: process batched messages
L328:     export class GameRoom extends DurableObject {
L329:     	async webSocketMessage(ws, message) {
L330:     		if (typeof message !== "string") return;
L331: 
L332:     		const batch = JSON.parse(message);
L333: 
L334:     		// Process all messages in the batch in a single handler invocation
L335:     		for (const msg of batch.messages) {
L336:     			this.handleMessage(ws, msg);
L337:     		}
L338:     	}
L339: 
L340:     	handleMessage(ws, msg) {
L341:     		// Handle individual message logic
L342:     	}
L343:     }`

L384: #### Why batching helps
L385: 
L386: WebSocket reads require context switches between the kernel and JavaScript runtime. Each individual message triggers this overhead. Batching 10-100 logical messages into a single WebSocket frame reduces context switches proportionally.
L387: 
L388: For high-frequency data like sensor readings or game state updates, use time-based or count-based batching. Batch every 50-100ms or every 50-100 messages, whichever comes first.
L389: 
L390: Note
L391: Hibernation is only supported when a Durable Object acts as a WebSocket server. Outgoing WebSockets do not hibernate.
L392: 
L393: However, an active outbound WebSocket connection keeps the Durable Object alive and prevents eviction for up to 15 minutes per connection. Refer to cite4†Lifecycle of a Durable Object for more information.
L394: Events such as cite18†alarms , incoming requests, and scheduled callbacks prevent hibernation. This includes `setTimeout` and `setInterval` usage. Read more about cite71†when a Durable Object incurs duration charges .
L395: ### Extended methods
L396: 
L397: The following methods are available on the Hibernation WebSocket API. Use them to persist and restore state before and after hibernation.
L398: #### `WebSocket.serializeAttachment`
L399: 
L400:   * `serializeAttachment(value `any`)` : `void`
L401: 
L402: Keeps a copy of `value` associated with the WebSocket connection.
L403: 
L404: Key behaviors:
L405:   * Serialized attachments persist through hibernation as long as the WebSocket remains healthy
L406:   * If either side closes the connection, attachments are lost
L407:   * Modifications to `value` after calling this method are not retained unless you call it again
L408:   * The `value` can be any type supported by the cite72†structured clone algorithm ↗†developer.mozilla.org L409:   * Maximum serialized size is 16,384 bytes
L410: For larger values or data that must persist beyond WebSocket lifetime, use the cite16†Storage API and store the corresponding key as an attachment.
L411: #### `WebSocket.deserializeAttachment`
L412: 
L413:   * `deserializeAttachment()`: `any`
L414: 
L415: Retrieves the most recent value passed to `serializeAttachment()`, or `null` if none exists.
L416: #### Attachment example
L417: Use `serializeAttachment` and `deserializeAttachment` to persist per-connection state across hibernation:
L418: 
L419:     `import { DurableObject } from "cloudflare:workers";
L420: 
L421:     export class WebSocketServer extends DurableObject {
L422:     	async fetch(request) {
L423:     		const url = new URL(request.url);
L424:     		const orderId = url.searchParams.get("orderId") ?? "anonymous";
L425: 
L426:     		const webSocketPair = new WebSocketPair();
L427:     		const [client, server] = Object.values(webSocketPair);
L428:     		this.ctx.acceptWebSocket(server);
L429: 
L430:     		// Persist per-connection state that survives hibernation
L431:     		const state = {
L432:     			orderId,
L433:     			joinedAt: Date.now(),
L434:     		};
L435:     		server.serializeAttachment(state);
L436: 
L437:     		return new Response(null, { status: 101, webSocket: client });
L438:     	}
L439: 
L440:     	async webSocketMessage(ws, message) {
L441:     		// Restore state after potential hibernation
L442:     		const state = ws.deserializeAttachment();
L443:     		ws.send(`Hello ${state.orderId}, you joined at ${state.joinedAt}`);
L444:     	}
L445: 
L446:     	async webSocketClose(ws, code, reason, wasClean) {
L447:     		const state = ws.deserializeAttachment();
L448:     		console.log(`${state.orderId} disconnected`);
L449:     		// With web_socket_auto_reply_to_close (compat date >= 2026-04-07), the runtime
L450:     		// auto-replies to Close frames. Calling close() is safe but no longer required.
L451:     		ws.close(code, reason);
L452:     	}
L453:     }`

L495: ## WebSocket Standard API
L496: 
L497: WebSocket connections are established by making an HTTP GET request with the `Upgrade: websocket` header.
L498: 
L499: The typical flow:
L500: 
L501:   1. A Worker validates the upgrade request
L502:   2. The Worker proxies the request to the Durable Object
L503:   3. The Durable Object accepts the server side connection
L504:   4. The Worker returns the client side connection in the response
L505: 
L506: Validate requests in a Worker
L507: Both Workers and Durable Objects are billed based on the number of requests. Validate requests in your Worker to avoid billing for invalid requests against a Durable Object.
L508: 
L509:     `// Worker
L510:     export default {
L511:     	async fetch(request, env, ctx) {
L512:     		if (request.method === "GET" && request.url.endsWith("/websocket")) {
L513:     			// Expect to receive a WebSocket Upgrade request.

L124: Vercel Functions natively support WebSocket connections for realtime features such as interactive AI streaming, chat, and collaborative apps.
L125: Established connections are pinned to the Function for its cite38†maximum duration . Future connections are not guaranteed to connect to the same Function. For durable state across WebSocket connections, we recommend using cite39†Redis from the Vercel Marketplace .

L101: Note
L102: 
L103: This page documents the storage API for the newer SQLite-backed Durable Objects.
L104: 
L105: For the legacy KV-backed Durable Object storage API, refer to cite17†KV-backed Durable Object Storage (Legacy) .
L106: The Durable Object Storage API allows Durable Objects to access transactional and strongly consistent storage. A Durable Object's attached storage is private to its unique instance and cannot be accessed by other objects.
L107: 
L108: The Durable Object Storage API comes with several methods, including SQL, point-in-time recovery (PITR), key-value (KV), and alarm APIs. Available API methods depend on the storage backend for a Durable Objects class, either cite63†SQLite or cite64†KV .
L109: Methods ^{1}  | SQLite-backed Durable Object class  | KV-backed Durable Object class
L110: --- | --- | ---
L111: SQL API  | ✅  | ❌
L112: PITR API  | ✅  | ❌
L113: Synchronous KV API  | ✅ ^{2, 3}  | ❌
L114: Asynchronous KV API  | ✅ ^{3}  | ✅
L115: Alarms API  | ✅  | ✅
L116: 
L117: Footnotes
L118: 
L119: ^{1} Each method is implicitly wrapped inside a transaction, such that its results are atomic and isolated from all other storage operations, even when accessing multiple key-value pairs.
L120: ^{2} KV API methods like `get()`, `put()`, `delete()`, or `list()` store data in a hidden SQLite table `__cf_kv`. Note that you will be able to view this table when listing all tables, but you will not be able to access its content through the SQL API.
L121: 
L122: ^{3} SQLite-backed Durable Objects also use cite65†synchronous KV API methods using `ctx.storage.kv`, whereas KV-backed Durable Objects only provide cite66†asynchronous KV API methods .
L123: 
L124: Recommended SQLite-backed Durable Objects
L125: Cloudflare recommends all new Durable Object namespaces use the cite63†SQLite storage backend . These Durable Objects can continue to use storage cite65†key-value API .
L126: 
L127: Additionally, SQLite-backed Durable Objects allow you to store more types of data (such as tables), and offer Point In Time Recovery API which can restore a Durable Object's embedded SQLite database contents (both SQL data and key-value data) to any point in the past 30 days.
L128: Creating new namespaces with the cite67†key-value storage backend is no longer supported for accounts without an existing key-value-backed namespace. The key-value storage backend remains available for existing namespaces, and a migration path from the key-value storage backend to the SQLite storage backend will be available in the future.
L129: 
L130: Storage billing on SQLite-backed Durable Objects
L131: Storage billing for SQLite-backed Durable Objects will be enabled in January 2026, with a target date of January 7, 2026 (no earlier). Only SQLite storage usage on and after the billing target date will incur charges. For more information, refer to cite68†Billing for SQLite Storage .
L132: ## Access storage
L133: 
L134: Durable Objects gain access to Storage API via the `DurableObjectStorage` interface and accessed by the `DurableObjectState::storage` property. This is frequently accessed via `this.ctx.storage` with the `ctx` parameter passed to the Durable Object constructor.
L135: The following code snippet shows you how to store and retrieve data using the Durable Object Storage API.
L136: 
L137:     `export class Counter extends DurableObject {
L138:     	constructor(ctx, env) {
L139:     		super(ctx, env);
L140:     	}
L141: 
L142:     	async increment() {
L143:     		let value = (await this.ctx.storage.get("value")) || 0;
L144:     		value += 1;
L145:     		await this.ctx.storage.put("value", value);
L146:     		return value;
L147:     	}
L148:     }`
L149: 
L150:     `export class Counter extends DurableObject {
L151:       constructor(ctx: DurableObjectState, env: Env) {
L152:         super(ctx, env);
L153:       }
L154: 
L155:         async increment(): Promise<number> {
L156:           let value: number = (await this.ctx.storage.get('value')) || 0;
L157:           value += 1;
L158:           await this.ctx.storage.put('value', value);
L159:           return value;
L160:         }
L161: 
L162:     }`
L163: 
L164:     `from workers import DurableObject
L165: 
L166:     class Counter(DurableObject):
L167:       def __init__(self, ctx, env):
L168:         super().__init__(ctx, env)
L169:       async def increment(self):
L170:         value = (await self.ctx.storage.get('value')) or 0
L171:         value += 1
L172:         await self.ctx.storage.put('value', value)
L173:         return value`
L174: JavaScript is a single-threaded and event-driven programming language. This means that JavaScript runtimes, by default, allow requests to interleave with each other which can lead to concurrency bugs. The Durable Objects runtime uses a combination of input gates and output gates to avoid this type of concurrency bug when performing storage operations. Learn more in our cite69†blog post ↗†blog.cloudflare.com .
L175: ## SQL API
L176: 
L177: The `SqlStorage` interface encapsulates methods that modify the SQLite database embedded within a Durable Object. The `SqlStorage` interface is accessible via the cite70†`sql` property of `DurableObjectStorage` class.
L178: For example, using `sql.exec()` a user can create a table and insert rows.
L179: 
L180:     `import { DurableObject } from "cloudflare:workers";
L181: 
L182:     export class MyDurableObject extends DurableObject {
L183:       sql: SqlStorage;
L184:       constructor(ctx: DurableObjectState, env: Env) {
L185:         super(ctx, env);
L186:         this.sql = ctx.storage.sql;
L187: 
L188:         this.sql.exec(`
L189:           CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS artist(
L190:             artistid    INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
L191:             artistname  TEXT
L192:           );
L193:           INSERT INTO artist (artistid, artistname) VALUES
L194:             (123, 'Alice'),
L195:             (456, 'Bob'),
L196:             (789, 'Charlie');
L197:         `);
L198:       }
L199:     }`
L200: 
L201:     `from workers import DurableObject
L202: 
L203:     class MyDurableObject(DurableObject):
L204:       def __init__(self, ctx, env):
L205:         super().__init__(ctx, env)
L206:         self.sql = ctx.storage.sql
L207: 
L208:         self.sql.exec("""
L209:           CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS artist(
L210:             artistid    INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
L211:             artistname  TEXT
L212:           );
L213:           INSERT INTO artist (artistid, artistname) VALUES
L214:             (123, 'Alice'),
L215:             (456, 'Bob'),
L216:             (789, 'Charlie');
L217:         """)`
L218:   * SQL API methods accessed with `ctx.storage.sql` are only allowed on cite63†Durable Object classes with SQLite storage backend and will return an error if called on Durable Object classes with a KV-storage backend.
L219:   * When writing data, every row update of an index counts as an additional row. However, indexes may be beneficial for read-heavy use cases. Refer to cite71†Index for SQLite Durable Objects .
L220:   * Writing data to cite72†SQLite virtual tables ↗†www.sqlite.org also counts towards rows written.
L221: Durable Objects support a subset of SQLite extensions for added functionality, including:
L222: 
L223:   * cite73†FTS5 module ↗†www.sqlite.org for full-text search (including `fts5vocab`).
L224:   * cite74†JSON extension ↗†www.sqlite.org for JSON functions and operators.
L225:   * cite75†Math functions ↗†sqlite.org .
L226: 
L227: Refer to the cite76†source code ↗†github.com for the full list of supported functions.
L228: ### `exec`
L229: 
L230: `exec(query: `string`, ...bindings: `any[]`)`: `SqlStorageCursor`
L231: #### Parameters
L232:   * `query`: `string`
L233:     * The SQL query string to be executed. `query` can contain `?` placeholders for parameter bindings. Multiple SQL statements, separated with a semicolon, can be executed in the `query`. With multiple SQL statements, any parameter bindings are applied to the last SQL statement in the `query`, and the returned cursor is only for the last SQL statement.
L234:   * `...bindings`: `any[]` Optional
L235:     * Optional variable number of arguments that correspond to the `?` placeholders in `query`.
L236: #### Returns

Yes. WebSockets are a strong fit, but they need durable storage behind them.

I recommend **Cloudflare Durable Objects + WebSockets**:

```text
Phone A ─┐
Phone B ─┼─ WebSocket ─ Worker ─ One Durable Object per room
Phone C ─┘                         └─ Durable SQLite storage
```

Each room gets one globally addressable Durable Object that:

- Maintains WebSocket connections for every participant.
- Broadcasts joins, vote progress, and the final result instantly.
- Stores participants and private votes in durable SQLite.
- Survives restarts, deployments, disconnects, and reconnects.
- Keeps each room’s updates coordinated without race conditions.

Cloudflare supports hibernating WebSockets, allowing connections to remain established while idle without continuously running the room process. [Cloudflare WebSockets](https://developers.cloudflare.com/durable-objects/best-practices/websockets/) Durable Object storage is transactional and strongly consistent. [Durable SQLite storage](https://developers.cloudflare.com/durable-objects/api/sqlite-storage-api/)

Another option is Vercel WebSockets plus Redis. Vercel supports WebSockets, but connections remain pinned only for a Function’s maximum duration, future connections may reach different Functions, and Vercel recommends Redis for durable state. [Vercel WebSocket guidance](https://vercel.com/kb/guide/do-vercel-serverless-functions-support-websocket-connections) That is more moving pieces than a Durable Object per dinner room.

I recommend we use:

- **Next.js** for the Girl Dinner website.
- **Cloudflare Worker** as the WebSocket gateway.
- **One SQLite-backed Durable Object per room** for persistence and coordination.
- **Google Places and Jev** through protected server endpoints.

I’ll remove the temporary in-memory room implementation and replace it with this production architecture. The only external requirement will be a Cloudflare account and API token when we are ready to deploy it. Is Cloudflare acceptable?

L101: Durable Objects can incur two types of billing: compute and storage.
L102: 
L103: Note
L104: 
L105: Durable Objects are available both on Workers Free and Workers Paid plans.
L106:   * Workers Free plan: Only Durable Objects with cite63†SQLite storage backend are available.
L107:   * Workers Paid plan: Durable Objects with the SQLite storage backend are available. The cite64†key-value storage backend is only available to accounts that already have a key-value-backed namespace.
L108: 
L109: If you wish to downgrade from a Workers Paid plan to a Workers Free plan, you must first ensure that you have deleted all Durable Object namespaces with the key-value storage backend.
L110: 
L111: On Workers Free plan:
L112:   * If you exceed any one of the free tier limits, further operations of that type will fail with an error.
L113:   * Daily free limits reset at 00:00 UTC.
L114: ## Compute billing
L115: 
L116: Durable Objects are billed for compute duration (wall-clock time) while the Durable Object is actively running or is idle in memory but unable to cite4†hibernate . Durable Objects that are idle and eligible for hibernation are not billed for duration, even before the runtime has hibernated them. Requests to a Durable Object keep it active or create the object if it was inactive.
L117: For each metered dimension, billable usage is the amount consumed in excess of the included monthly allocation. This billable usage is rounded up to the next billable unit before the corresponding rate is applied. For example, 500,000 GB-s of billable compute duration is rounded up to 1,000,000 GB-s and billed accordingly.
L118:  | Free plan  | Paid plan
L119: --- | --- | ---
L120: Requests  | 100,000 / day  | 1 million / month, + $0.15/million
L121: Includes HTTP requests, RPC sessions^{1}, WebSocket messages^{2}, and alarm invocations
L122: Duration^{3}  | 13,000 GB-s / day  | 400,000 GB-s / month, + $12.50/million GB-s^{4,5}
L123: 
L124: Footnotes
L125: 
L126: ^{1} Each cite65†RPC session is billed as one request to your Durable Object. Every cite6†RPC method call on a cite1†Durable Objects stub is its own RPC session and therefore a single billed request.
L127: RPC method calls can return objects (stubs) extending cite66†`RpcTarget` and invoke calls on those stubs. Subsequent calls on the returned stub are part of the same RPC session and are not billed as separate requests. For example:
L128: 
L129:     `let durableObjectStub = OBJECT_NAMESPACE.get(id); // retrieve Durable Object stub
L130:     using foo = await durableObjectStub.bar(); // billed as a request
L131:     await foo.baz(); // treated as part of the same RPC session created by calling bar(), not billed as a request
L132:     await durableObjectStub.cat(); // billed as a request`
L133: ^{2} A request is needed to create a WebSocket connection. There is no charge for outgoing WebSocket messages, nor for incoming cite67†WebSocket protocol pings ↗†www.rfc-editor.org . For compute requests billing-only, a 20:1 ratio is applied to incoming WebSocket messages to factor in smaller messages for real-time communication. For example, 100 WebSocket incoming messages would be charged as 5 requests for billing purposes.
L134: The 20:1 ratio does not affect Durable Object metrics and analytics, which reflect actual usage.
L135: ^{3} Application level auto-response messages handled by cite8†`state.setWebSocketAutoResponse()` will not incur additional wall-clock time, and so they will not be charged.
L136: ^{4} Duration is billed in wall-clock time as long as the Object is active and not eligible for hibernation, but is shared across all requests active on an Object at once. Calling `accept()` on a WebSocket in an Object will incur duration charges for the entire time the WebSocket is connected. It is recommended to use the WebSocket Hibernation API to avoid incurring duration charges once all event handlers finish running.
L137: For a complete explanation, refer to cite68†When does a Durable Object incur duration charges? .
L138: ^{5} Duration billing charges for the 128 MB of memory your Durable Object is allocated, regardless of actual usage. If your account creates many instances of a single Durable Object class, Durable Objects may run in the same isolate on the same physical machine and share the 128 MB of memory. These Durable Objects are still billed as if they are allocated a full 128 MB of memory.
L139: ## Storage billing
L140: 
L141: The cite16†Durable Objects Storage API is only accessible from within Durable Objects. Pricing depends on the storage backend of your Durable Objects.
L142: 
L143:   * SQLite-backed Durable Objects (recommended): cite63†SQLite storage backend is recommended for all new Durable Object classes. Workers Free plan can only create and access SQLite-backed Durable Objects.
L144:   * Key-value backed Durable Objects: cite69†Key-value storage backend is only available on the Workers Paid plan.
L145: ### SQLite storage backend
L146: 
L147: Storage billing on SQLite-backed Durable Objects
L148: 
L149: Storage billing for SQLite-backed Durable Objects will be enabled in January 2026, with a target date of January 7, 2026 (no earlier). Only SQLite storage usage on and after the billing target date will incur charges. For more information, refer to cite70†Billing for SQLite Storage .
L150:  | Workers Free plan  | Workers Paid plan
L151: --- | --- | ---
L152: Rows reads ^{1,2}  | 5 million / day  | First 25 billion / month included + $0.001 / million rows
L153: Rows written ^{1,2,3,4}  | 100,000 / day  | First 50 million / month included + $1.00 / million rows
L154: SQL Stored data ^{5}  | 5 GB (total)  | 5 GB-month, + $0.20/ GB-month
L155: 
L156: Footnotes
L157: 
L158: ^{1} Rows read and rows written included limits and rates match cite71†D1 pricing , Cloudflare's serverless SQL database.
L159: ^{2} Key-value methods like `get()`, `put()`, `delete()`, or `list()` store and query data in a hidden SQLite table and are billed as rows read and rows written.
L160: 
L161: ^{3} Each `setAlarm()` is billed as a single row written.
L162: 
L163: ^{4} Deletes are counted as rows written.
L164: 
L165: ^{5} Durable Objects will be billed for stored data until the cite72†data is removed . Once the data is removed, the object will be cleaned up automatically by the system.
L166: ### Key-value storage backend
L167: 
L168:  | Workers Paid plan
L169: --- | ---
L170: Read request units^{1,2}  | 1 million, + $0.20/million
L171: Write request units^{3}  | 1 million, + $1.00/million
L172: Delete requests^{4}  | 1 million, + $1.00/million
L173: Stored data^{5}  | 1 GB, + $0.20/ GB-month
L174: 
L175: Footnotes
L176: 
L177: ^{1} A request unit is defined as 4 KB of data read or written. A request that writes or reads more than 4 KB will consume multiple units, for example, a 9 KB write will consume 3 write request units.
L178: ^{2} List operations are billed by read request units, based on the amount of data examined. For example, a list request that returns a combined 80 KB of keys and values will be billed 20 read request units. A list request that does not return anything is billed for 1 read request unit.
L179: 
L180: ^{3} Each `setAlarm` is billed as a single write request unit.
L181: 
L182: ^{4} Delete requests are unmetered. For example, deleting a 100 KB value will be charged one delete request.
L183: ^{5} Durable Objects will be billed for stored data until the data is removed. Once the data is removed, the object will be cleaned up automatically by the system.
L184: 
L185: Requests that hit the cite43†Durable Objects in-memory cache or that use the cite16†multi-key versions of `get()`/`put()`/`delete()` methods are billed the same as if they were a normal, individual request for each key.
L186: ## Compute billing examples
L187: 
L188: These examples exclude the costs for the Workers calling the Durable Objects. When modelling the costs of a Durable Object, note that:
L189:   * Inactive objects receiving no requests do not incur any duration charges.
L190:   * The cite73†WebSocket Hibernation API can dramatically reduce duration-related charges for Durable Objects communicating with clients over the WebSocket protocol, especially if messages are only transmitted occasionally at sparse intervals.
L191:     * An active outbound connection (via cite74†`connect()` or an outbound WebSocket) keeps a Durable Object in memory and causes it to incur duration charges for up to 15 minutes per connection, even with no incoming requests. Refer to cite4†Lifecycle of a Durable Object for more information.
L192: ### Example 1
L193: 
L194: This example represents a simple Durable Object used as a co-ordination service invoked via HTTP.
L195: 
L196:   * A single Durable Object was called by a Worker 1.5 million times
L197:   * It is active for 1,000,000 seconds in the month
L198: 
L199: In this scenario, the estimated monthly cost would be calculated as:
L200: 
L201: Requests:
L202: 
L203:   * 1.5 million requests - included 1 million requests = 500,000 billable requests.
L204:   * (rounded) 1,000,000 requests x $0.15 / 1,000,000 = $0.15.
L205: 
L206: Compute Duration:
L207:   * 1,000,000 seconds * 128 MB / 1 GB = 128,000 GB-s.
L208:   * 128,000 GB-s is within the 400,000 GB-s included allocation = $0.00.
L209: 
L210: Estimated total: $0.15 (requests) + $0.00 (compute duration) + minimum $5/mo usage = $5.15 per month
L211: ### Example 2
L212: 
L213: This example represents a moderately trafficked Durable Objects based application using WebSockets to broadcast game, chat or real-time user state across connected clients:
L214: 
L215:   * 100 Durable Objects have 50 WebSocket connections established to each of them.
L216:   * Clients send approximately one message a minute for eight active hours a day, every day of the month.
L217: 
L218: In this scenario, the estimated monthly cost would be calculated as:
L219: 
L220: Requests:
L221:   * 50 WebSocket connections * 100 Durable Objects to establish the WebSockets = 5,000 connections created each day * 30 days = 150,000 WebSocket connection requests.
L222:   * 50 messages per minute * 100 Durable Objects * 60 minutes * 8 hours * 30 days = 72,000,000 WebSocket message requests.
L223:   * 150,000 + (72 million requests / 20 for WebSocket message billing ratio) = 3.75 million billing request.
L224:   * 3.75 million requests - included 1 million requests = 2,750,000 billable requests.
L225:   * (rounded) 3,000,000 requests x $0.15 / 1,000,000 = $0.45.
L226: Compute Duration:
L227: 
L228:   * 100 Durable Objects * 60 seconds * 60 minutes * 8 hours * 30 days = 86,400,000 seconds.
L229:   * 86,400,000 seconds * 128 MB / 1 GB = 11,059,200 GB-s.
L230:   * 11,059,200 GB-s - included 400,000 GB-s = 10,659,200 GB-s
L231:   * (rounded) 11,000,000 GB-s x $12.50 / 1,000,000 = $137.50.
L232: 
L233: Estimated total: $0.45 (requests) + $137.50 (compute duration) + minimum $5/mo usage = $142.95 per month.
L234: ### Example 3
L235: 
L236: This example represents a horizontally scaled Durable Objects based application using WebSockets to communicate user-specific state to a single client connected to each Durable Object.
L237: 
L238:   * 100 Durable Objects each have a single WebSocket connection established to each of them.
L239:   * Clients sent one message every second of the month so that the Durable Objects were active for the entire month.
L240: 
L241: In this scenario, the estimated monthly cost would be calculated as:
L242: 
L243: Requests:
L244:   * 100 WebSocket connection requests.
L245:   * 1 message per second * 100 connections * 60 seconds * 60 minutes * 24 hours * 30 days = 259,200,000 WebSocket message requests.
L246:   * 100 + (259.2 million requests / 20 for WebSocket billing ratio) = 12,960,100 requests.
L247:   * 12,960,100 requests - included 1 million requests = 11,960,100 billable requests.
L248:   * (rounded) 12,000,000 requests x $0.15 / 1,000,000 = $1.80.
L249: 
L250: Compute Duration:
L251:   * 100 Durable Objects * 60 seconds * 60 minutes * 24 hours * 30 days = 259,200,000 seconds
L252:   * 259,200,000 seconds * 128 MB / 1 GB = 33,177,600 GB-s
L253:   * 33,177,600 GB-s - included 400,000 GB-s = 32,777,600 GB-s
L254:   * (rounded) 33,000,000 GB-s x $12.50 / 1,000,000 = $412.50
L255: 
L256: Estimated total: $1.80 (requests) + $412.50 (compute duration) + minimum $5/mo usage = $419.30 per month
L257: ### Example 4
L258: 
L259: This example represents a moderately trafficked Durable Objects based application using WebSocket Hibernation to broadcast game, chat or real-time user state across connected clients:
L260:   * 100 Durable Objects each have 100 Hibernatable WebSocket connections established to each of them.
L261:   * Clients send one message per minute, and it takes 10ms to process a single message in the `webSocketMessage()` handler. Since each Durable Object handles 100 WebSockets, cumulatively each Durable Object will be actively executing JS for 1 second each minute (100 WebSockets * 10ms).
L262: 
L263: In this scenario, the estimated monthly cost would be calculated as:
L264: 
L265: Requests:
L266:   * 100 WebSocket connections * 100 Durable Objects to establish the WebSockets = 10,000 initial WebSocket connection requests.
L267:   * 100 messages per minute^{1} * 100 Durable Objects * 60 minutes * 24 hours * 30 days = 432,000,000 requests.
L268:   * 10,000 + (432 million requests / 20 for WebSocket billing ratio) = 21,610,000 million requests.
L269:   * 21,610,000 requests - included 1 million requests = 20,610,000 billable requests.
L270:   * (rounded) 21,000,000 requests x $0.15 / 1,000,000 = $3.15.
L271: 
L272: Compute Duration:
L273:   * 100 Durable Objects * 1 second^{2} * 60 minutes * 24 hours * 30 days = 4,320,000 seconds
L274:   * 4,320,000 seconds * 128 MB / 1 GB = 552,960 GB-s
L275:   * 552,960 GB-s - included 400,000 GB-s = 152,960 GB-s
L276:   * (rounded) 1,000,000 GB-s x $12.50 / 1,000,000 = $12.50
L277: 
L278: Estimated total: $3.15 (requests) + $12.50 (compute duration) + minimum $5/mo usage = $20.65 per month
L279: 
L280: ^{1} 100 messages per minute comes from the fact that 100 clients connect to each DO, and each sends 1 message per minute.
L281: ^{2} The example uses 1 second because each Durable Object is active for 1 second per minute. This can also be thought of as 432 million requests that each take 10 ms to execute (4,320,000 seconds).
L282: ## Frequently Asked Questions
L283: ### When does a Durable Object incur duration charges?
L284: 
L285: A Durable Object incurs duration charges when it is actively executing JavaScript — either handling a request or running event handlers — or when it is idle but does not meet the cite4†conditions for hibernation . An idle Durable Object that qualifies for hibernation does not incur duration charges, even during the brief window before the runtime hibernates it.
L286: Once an object has been evicted from memory, the next time it is needed, it will be recreated (calling the constructor again).
L287: 
L288: There are several factors that can prevent a Durable Object from hibernating and cause it to continue incurring duration charges.
L289: 
L290: Find more information in cite4†Lifecycle of a Durable Object .
L291: ### Does an empty table / SQLite database contribute to my storage?
L292: 
L293: Yes, although minimal. Empty tables can consume at least a few kilobytes, based on the number of columns (table width) in the table. An empty SQLite database consumes approximately 12 KB of storage.
L294: ### Does metadata stored in Durable Objects count towards my storage?
L295: 
L296: All writes to a SQLite-backed Durable Object stores nominal amounts of metadata in internal tables in the Durable Object, which counts towards your billable storage.
L297: 
L298: The metadata remains in the Durable Object until you call cite75†`deleteAll()` .

L236: ## cite96†Hobby billing cycle L237: 
L238: As the Hobby plan is a free tier there are no billing cycles. In most cases, if you exceed your usage limits on the Hobby plan, you will have to wait until 30 days have passed before you can use the feature again.
